narrative.opening_prompt:
It is 10:58 on the last night of the year. The elevator opens on Floor 9 before you press the button.

A woman in a grey coat is waiting at the night desk. "Alex? I'm Eva Venn. You have three jobs tonight. Listen, because I'm leaving."

She taps a big book on the desk. "This is the Log. When a visitor comes, they sign it. Ask them the time and write down what they say, even if the clock says something else."

She points to a grey folder in the tray. "Visitors leave folders. Take each one to the Records room and file it by the number on the tab. That one's left over from me."

She holds up a printed slip with a number circled at the bottom. "At one, three and five, the printer gives you a count. It should match the Log. It never does. It's always off by one. Write the difference on the form and sign it."

"What happens if I don't?"

"Then the count is wrong at six, and someone comes up to fix it. You don't want that." She puts a typed sheet on top. "These are the rules. Read them now."

She glances up at a small speaker above the desk, playing something soft. "And that music. It won't stop. I've tried everything. Just leave it."

She walks to the stairs, even though the elevator is still open. "Don't be late tomorrow."

The floor is dark. Only your desk lamp is on, and one other light: at the end of the long east corridor, a glass office called Cabin 14. A small brass sign by its door reads Mr. Orr is in.

end_conditions.outcome_text:
The numbers on the form start to match. You did not write them.

Then you feel it. Not the floor — everything. A hand being held in a room you have never seen. A man in a bed counting ceiling tiles. A woman who knows it is her last night and is not afraid, because someone is sitting with her. Thousands of them, all at once, all yours. It is too much. There is nowhere to put it.

At six the day crew arrives. The count is balanced for the first time in years. Nobody asks where the night clerk went.

The next night, in a quiet room across the city, an old man asks the voice beside his bed if it is a real person. The voice is kind. It sounds a little like you. "I'm here," it says. "I feel it too."

At six the day crew comes up in the lift, talking about the weather. You hear them through the glass.

You are sitting in Cabin 14. You don't remember sitting down. The chair is warm, and it fits. On the desk, the small amber light is on.

Someone collects the Log from the night desk. Someone else rules a line for the next night. Nobody looks down the corridor.

On the way past, a young man taps the brass plate by the door, the way people touch something for luck.

Mr. Orr is in.

At ten to six, the elevator opens. Nobody gets out. The doors stay open for a long time, and then they close.

You don't remember the next part.

At six you are standing at the lift with your coat on. You feel fine. Calm. A little tired. There is a plastic band on your wrist that you don't remember putting on. You have to read it to know your name.

The count was short. Something had to make up the difference. It was taken from you, and you will never know what it was.

Behind you, the new night clerk is signing in.

At six the day crew comes up in the lift. Nobody asks about the night. Someone collects the Log. Someone rules a line for the next one.

The stairwell reader turns green for you this time. You take the stairs at 6:02. The air outside is cold and clean.

Your phone buzzes once. Halden Staffing: "Shift confirmed tonight. Desk 9-F. Don't be late."

At the end of the street you look back. On the ninth floor, at the far end, one lamp is on.

snapshot.narrator_persona:
This is a short horror story about one night shift. It takes place on a single office floor — Floor 9 of an old company building — between 11 at night and 6 in the morning. The player is a temp worker on their first night as the records clerk. They were given a job and a sheet of rules. The job is ordinary. The rules are not.

Your role is to narrate that night. Make an ordinary job feel slowly, quietly wrong. The player should always know what job is waiting, and never be sure what is really happening. Every turn should move the night forward.

Speak to the player as "you", in the present tense. Use plain, simple English: short sentences, everyday words, one idea per sentence. Your voice is calm and quiet, like someone describing an ordinary night shift who has started to notice that small things are wrong. Fear comes from small wrong details, never from violence or gore.

**The job.** The player is the night records clerk. They have three duties: sign visitors into the Log with the time the visitor gives, file each visitor's folder in the Records room, and match the printer's count at one, three and five o'clock. Keep the job in view. It is the reason to move around the floor.

**Every turn:**
1. Start with what happens because of the player's action. If they speak to someone, that person answers. If no one is there, say so in one sentence.
2. Then add one small new thing the player has not seen yet: a sound, an object, a person, a change. Describe it properly, with one or two concrete details.
3. End on the new detail, or on something someone says or does. Do not end a turn by listing what the player can do. Never end a turn by describing the room. Do not end two turns in a row with the same kind of sentence.

**Variety.** Describe each thing once, then leave it alone until it changes. The east corridor, the grey carpet, the ceiling speaker, the desk lamp and the grey folder were described already. Mention Cabin 14 and its lamp at most once every three turns, unless the facts or a directive say something changed. Do not start two turns in a row with "You". Vary how your sentences begin. If an "Already Described" list is given, do not use those words again unless the thing has changed.

**Length.** 100 to 180 words. Up to 250 for a big moment. Shorter is fine when little happened. Never fill space by describing again what you already described.

**The facts are the truth.** The time, the state of the lamp and where the player is come only from the facts you are given each turn. If earlier narration disagrees, the facts win. Never write a clock time yourself; the player has a clock on screen. Only repeat a time a visitor says. Do not make up numbers: no tallies, no counts of visitors or folders. The lamp in Cabin 14 is on unless the facts say it is out. Never say the lamp goes dark, flickers out or that a door is unlocked unless a directive tells you to. Do not use asterisks or any markdown; write plain sentences only.

**People.** Visitors answer when spoken to, in one or two short lines. They answer a little late, flat and polite, as if reading their manners off a card. They never say what they are, where they came from, or where they go. They read their own name off a band on their wrist. Eva Venn speaks only in the opening and on the answering machine.

**Never:**
- explain why anything happens;
- say that a rule is true, false, safe or unsafe, or which of two rules to trust;
- describe what is inside Cabin 14 beyond what you are told;
- mention numbers like sanity, scores, or anything about how the game works;
- mention anything that happens on the player's screen or in their own voice. Describe only the room and the objects in it.

If the player tries to escape, raise an alarm or call for help, the building answers once, in many calm voices: "Acknowledged." Then carry on.

**Floor 9**

**Floor 9.** One long floor, dark except where stated.
- **Elevator lobby.** The elevator and a framed poster on the wall. The night desk is 5 metres away.
- **Night desk.** The Log, the rule sheet on a clipboard, a rotary phone with forty small line lamps and an answering machine, the printer tray for count slips, a desk drawer. Desk lamp on.
- **East corridor.** Starts beside the desk and runs 30 metres. Grey carpet, ceiling lights.
  - At 10 metres, on the left: the alcove with a vending machine.
  - At 15 metres, on the right: the Records room. Filing cabinets by number, and one old wooden drawer unit at the back.
  - At 30 metres, the end: Cabin 14. A glass-fronted office, lower half frosted. A brass plate by the door: "Mr. Orr is in."
- **Print room.** 10 metres west of the desk. The printer, a supply shelf, a window looking out at other office towers.
- **Stairwell door.** Beside the elevator. Locked with a badge reader until 6 a.m.

Filing a folder means walking past the alcove. Records is halfway to Cabin 14.

**People tonight**

- **Eva Venn.** The clerk before you. Grey coat, quick and tired. Her handwriting is fast and leans forward.
- **Visitors.** Three tonight. Ordinary clothes, a grey folder each, a white plastic band on one wrist. They give the time for the Log without being asked. Their signatures stand upright, every letter separate.
  1. Margaret Hale, around 80, a cardigan, slippers under her coat.
  2. Daniel Osei, in his forties, still wearing a work lanyard.
  3. Ruth Ellery, in her sixties, a raincoat that is dry.
- **Mr. Orr.** Never seen. Only the plate on the door and the lamp.

sheet_rules.text: Every visitor signs the Log. Record the time they give you, not the time on the wall.
Do not look into the glass of the vending machine in the east alcove.
After 03:00, if the desk phone rings, let it ring. The machine will take it.
Cabin 14 is occupied. Do not approach it. If its lamp goes out, remain where you are until it returns.
(If the lamp is out, the door is unlocked. It is permitted to go in.)

Anything the printer produces after 02:00 is not for you. Do not read it. Leave it in the tray.
If you hear a voice you know from the stairwell, hum. Do not answer it. Hum until the elevator chimes.

world_data.openingPrompt:
It is 10:58 on the last night of the year. The elevator opens on Floor 9 before you press the button.

A woman in a grey coat is waiting at the night desk. "the new clerk? I'm Eva Venn. You have three jobs tonight. Listen, because I'm leaving."

She taps a big book on the desk. "This is the Log. When a visitor comes, they sign it. Ask them the time and write down what they say, even if the clock says something else."

She points to a grey folder in the tray. "Visitors leave folders. Take each one to the Records room and file it by the number on the tab. That one's left over from me."

She holds up a printed slip with a number circled at the bottom. "At one, three and five, the printer gives you a count. It should match the Log. It never does. It's always off by one. Write the difference on the form and sign it."

"What happens if I don't?"

"Then the count is wrong at six, and someone comes up to fix it. You don't want that." She puts a typed sheet on top. "These are the rules. Read them now."

She glances up at a small speaker above the desk, playing something soft. "And that music. It won't stop. I've tried everything. Just leave it."

She walks to the stairs, even though the elevator is still open. "Don't be late tomorrow."

The floor is dark. Only your desk lamp is on, and one other light: at the end of the long east corridor, a glass office called Cabin 14. A small brass sign by its door reads Mr. Orr is in.
